rv.q: The play is not an endorsement of violence; it's a cautionary tale about its risks.

Years before “Everybody Loves Raymond” propelled Brad Garrett to stardom, he was a stand-up comedian opening for Frank Sinatra in Las Vegas. He capped his warm-up act on one particularly unresponsive night by deadpanning: “You’re a great audience. Stick around for Frank.”
It's a staging for this age, if not the ages.

Its would-be provocative central conceit notwithstanding, this is a bland, unevenly acted production of Shakespeare's play whose main virtues are its fast pace — it runs two hours without an intermission — and vigorous energy.
The Public’s production is less interested in setting up a perfect analogy than it is in using Caesar as a jumping-off point, sparking discussion about power and justice.
Eustis, directing at Shakespeare in the Park for the first time in nearly a decade, isn’t going for subtlety with this “Julius Caesar.”

More often than not, the hyper-contemporary Trumpian veneer that’s been slathered over this production like a gold paint carwash does end up amplifying fleeting moments of close connection to our present day, but it does so at the expense of the play’s larger message.

This heavy-handed, uncomfortable and unnecessary stroke of provocation on the part of Eustis (who rarely directs shows himself) turns what might have otherwise been a decent Shakespeare in the Park production into a jumbled mess.

cn.t: This Trump-styled Julius Caesar divides critics between those who find it a timely, well-executed political allegory and those who dismiss the concept as heavy-handed provocation that overshadows the production itself.
